episodes.title_en: The House of Wisdom: how Baghdad became a city of books
episodes.intro_en: Today: how Baghdad became a city of books, and why a caliph dreamed of Aristotle.
sections: Baghdad is a new city. The caliph al-Mansur builds it beside the river Tigris as a round city, more than twelve hundred years ago. It quickly becomes rich and very large, and people come to it from many countries with their languages and their books.

The caliph Harun al-Rashid and then his son al-Ma'mun love knowledge. In the palace there is a library called the House of Wisdom (Bayt al-Hikma), where scholars read, write and work. Be honest that historians today do not agree on how big it really was: perhaps a great institution, perhaps just the caliph's library.

The translation movement. Old Greek books of medicine, mathematics and philosophy (Aristotle, Galen) are turned into Arabic, often by Christians who knew Greek and Syriac. The greatest translator is Hunayn ibn Ishaq, a Christian doctor, who travelled to look for a single book. The story says the caliph paid him the weight of each book in gold; A wonders if he then wrote on very heavy paper.

The dream of al-Ma'mun. The story: he sees in his sleep a man sitting on his bed, asks who he is, and the man says he is Aristotle. The caliph asks him: what is the good? Aristotle answers: what is good in the mind. A doubts the story is true. B: probably not, but the story shows what people of that time thought was important.

Why this matters today. Many Greek books were lost in Greek and lived only in Arabic. Centuries later they were translated from Arabic into Latin and reached Europe. So a book could travel from Athens to Baghdad to Spain. Close: tomorrow they will talk about the thing that made all these books possible and cheap: paper.

episodes.title_en: Paper: the cheap material that changed everything
episodes.intro_en: Today: how paper came to Baghdad, and the market where books were made and sold.
sections: Before paper. People wrote on papyrus, a plant from Egypt, or on the skin of animals. Skin is strong but very expensive: one big book needs the skins of a whole flock of sheep. So books were few and only the rich had them. A jokes about how many sheep her own bookshelf would cost.

Paper comes from China. The traditional story: after a battle in Central Asia, Chinese prisoners who knew how to make paper were taken to the city of Samarkand, and taught the people there. Historians doubt the story, but it is true that Samarkand became famous for its paper. Paper is made from old clothes and water, so it is cheap.

In the time of Harun al-Rashid paper is made in Baghdad itself. The government begins to write everything on paper. One reason is surprising: writing on skin can be washed off and changed, but on paper it cannot be changed without leaving a mark, so paper is safer against liars and thieves.

The market of the paper-sellers (the warraqun) in Baghdad: a street with more than a hundred shops. A warraq sells paper, copies books by hand, and sells books. The shops are also where scholars meet and talk. The writer al-Jahiz is said to have rented shops for the night so he could stay inside and read all the books.

How a book was published without printing. The author sits in the mosque and reads his book aloud; students write down every word; then a student reads his copy back to the author, who corrects it and gives permission to teach it. Result: libraries in Baghdad and Cordoba with many thousands of books, when the biggest libraries in Europe had a few hundred. Close: tomorrow, a bookseller who tried to write down the name of every book in the world.

episodes.title_en: Ibn al-Nadim and the list of every book
episodes.intro_en: Today: a Baghdad bookseller who tried to list every book ever written in Arabic.
sections: Ibn al-Nadim lives in Baghdad about a thousand years ago. His father sold books and he grows up in the shop, among books and the people who love them. He has a big idea: to write one book that lists every book that exists in Arabic, with who wrote it. The book is called al-Fihrist, which simply means the list.

What is in the list. It has ten parts: holy books, the Arabic language, history, poetry, religion and law, philosophy and the old sciences, stories, and more. For each writer he tells a little about his life, and he is honest: he says whether he saw the book with his own eyes or only heard about it from a man he trusts.

Surprising things in the list. He writes about books of stories told at night, and mentions an old Persian book of a thousand stories, the beginning of what we call the Thousand and One Nights: a king, and a woman who tells him a story every night so that he does not kill her. Ibn al-Nadim did not like it: he says he read it and it is a weak, cold book. He also writes about the religions of India and China, from what travellers told him.

The sad part. Most of the books in his list no longer exist. Fire, water, war and time took them. Later, an army from the east took Baghdad and destroyed its libraries; the famous story says so many books were thrown into the Tigris that the water of the river turned black from the ink. That story may not be true, but the loss is true. For thousands of books, the only thing we know is one line in his list.

Closing thoughts for the three days. Al-Jahiz, who loved books so much, wrote that a book is the friend who never makes you tired and never leaves you, and the legend says he died as an old man when a pile of his books fell on him. A: a good death for a reader. They agree that a list of lost books is also a kind of library, and say goodbye.
